title: Gender Pay Gap in the Board Room and Governance Attributes That Moderate the Gap
summary: ABSTRACT We examine whether there is a difference in the compensation paid to female and male directors of US firms and find that, on average, US female directors receive less total compensation than their male counterparts. Further, the gender pay gap is smaller on female‐friendly boards, a pattern consistent with the homophily principle and social identity theory. Despite the lower compensation, additional tests find that female directors are associated with higher financial reporting quality and marginally higher CEO compensation‐performance sensitivity, indicating that the pay gap is not explained by weaker monitoring. Among the governance attributes we examine, a female board chair is associated with the largest reduction in the gap, larger than that associated with a female CEO or a female‐majority board. The gap is also smaller when females hold a super majority, a configuration that is far less common in practice.

title: The role of the cluster approach in forming a competitive innovative business environment
summary: The article presents a theoretical and empirical analysis of the cluster approach as a key instrument for shaping a competitive, innovation-oriented business environment amid globalization and digital transformation. The article aims to conceptualize the role of cluster-based cooperation in fostering innovation, technological modernization, and firms’ international competitiveness, while also identifying barriers to implementing cluster policies effectively in Ukraine compared with the European Union. The research methodological framework combines system-structural, comparative, and institutional-evolutionary approaches, supported by statistical analysis of innovation activity among Ukrainian enterprises for 2018–2024. The study employs both a qualitative synthesis of theoretical models and a quantitative evaluation of innovation performance indicators, focusing on the correlation among cluster participation, R&D expenditures, and regional competitiveness. The findings reveal that in the context of the knowledge-based economy, the classical assumptions of cluster theory require revision: geographical proximity is no longer a decisive factor for success, especially in service and digital industries, where virtual and transregional clusters emerge through digital platforms and communication technologies. The research shows that modern clusters are evolving into complex, innovative ecosystems that integrate a broader range of actors and form flexible network structures that balance competition and cooperation. The article shows that in the European Union, clusters serve as strategic platforms for implementing smart specialization and fostering internationalization. Meanwhile, in post-socialist economies, including Ukraine, a lack of institutionalization and unified methodological standards limits their transformative potential. The article concludes that shifting to an ecosystem-based cluster model can enhance regional innovation capacity, attract foreign investment, and accelerate integration into global value chains. Keywords: cluster approach, innovation ecosystem, competitiveness, innovation policy, smart specialization, network interactions, institutional environment.

title: ESG Performance and Audit Quality: Bidirectional Relationship and the Moderator Role of Gender Diversity in an International Context
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines the bidirectional relationship between environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance and audit quality and the moderating role of board gender diversity. Using an international sample of 3630 firm‐year observations over 2017–2022, we estimate System GMM and generalized structural equation models. Audit quality is measured using audit fees and audit opinions. The results indicate that ESG performance is negatively associated with audit fees, whereas the reverse relationship is insignificant. This negative association extends to all three ESG pillars. ESG performance is unrelated to audit opinion in the full sample, but the association is positive for low‐ESG firms and negative for high‐ESG firms. By contrast, unmodified audit opinions are negatively associated with ESG performance and with all three ESG pillars. Board gender diversity moderates both directions of the ESG–audit fee relationship, attenuating the negative associations as female representation increases. For audit opinions, moderation occurs only from ESG performance to audit opinion. Overall, the findings reveal substantial heterogeneity across audit‐quality measures, ESG profiles, and board composition.

title: Digital transformation of regions and territorial communities of Ukraine: problems and ways to solve them
summary: The article examines the challenges of digital transformation in Ukraine’s regions and territorial communities amid full-scale war and limited organizational and investment resources. The article identifies significant spatial digital divides between regions and territorial communities, as well as between regional centers and peripheral communities. Data from the Digital Transformation Index of the Regions of Ukraine for 2024–2025 reveal a polarization in digital development, and the “Digital Economy” sub-index is one of the index’s weakest components. The key problems of digitalization have been characterized, in particular: the destruction of digital infrastructure in frontline territories, residual financing of informatization in communities, communities’ low capacity to attract investment resources, a shortage of IT specialists, a deteriorating demographic situation, including changes in the age structure of the population of rural communities, and cybersecurity threats. The authors propose directions and tools to address these problems within Ukraine’s post-war recovery strategy. The authors argue that the digitalization of public administration and the digitalization of the economy are relatively autonomous processes that develop at different rates and with different effectiveness. The following directions for solving the identified problems have been proposed: state support for the development of digital infrastructure in mountainous and frontline territories, reducing the energy dependence of telecommunications, developing local digital education hubs, expanding the Trembita system and introducing standard digital solutions for communities, developing e-democracy tools, and supporting the digitalization of small and medium-sized enterprises through the Diia. Business network, regional IT clusters, and co-financing programs. Under wartime conditions, digitalization has proven to be a factor in regions’ security capacity and should be an integral part of Ukraine’s Recovery Plan and the strategy for integration into the EU Digital Single Market. Keywords: sustainable regional development, territorial community, local authorities, decentralization, cooperation, organizational and administrative mechanism, strategic planning, local budgets, digital technologies, public-private partnership, European integration.

title: Smart strategies for a sustainable future: Bridging green finance, smart technologies, and sustainable energy efficiency to combat environmental degradation
summary: Rising environmental degradation (ED) is a global phenomenon. While various environmental initiatives have been introduced across disciplines, mitigating environmental degradation remains a critical challenge. Recently, the world has emphasized the importance of smart technologies, green finance, and stringent government policies as additional tools for environmental sustainability; therefore, it is essential to clarify the empirical evidence on their effectiveness for environmental policymakers. This study evaluates income, population in large cities, smart technologies, green finance, sustainable energy efficiency, and government policy as environmental determinants for nine OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) nations from 2012 to 2023. Using panel quantile regression and fully modified ordinary least squares, the empirical findings reveal that the population of large cities and sustainable energy efficiency are positively associated with ED. Conversely, income shows an inverse connection and contributes to sustainability. In the context of smart technologies, this study focuses on digital transformation (DT) and artificial intelligence and finds a significant role for DT in environmental management. This study employs two proxies for green finance: green foreign direct investment and green bonds, both of which exhibit unusual behavior with respect to the intended theme. Finally, the moderating effect of green finance and smart technologies on sustainable energy efficiency doesn't support environmental management. This study also offers valuable suggestions for achieving long-term environmental sustainability.

title: Fuzzy–AI digital twins for sustainable, resilient food supply chains
summary: This study proposes a prescriptive Fuzzy–AI Digital Twin framework for food supply chains operating under deep uncertainty. The digital twin streams real-time operational data from production, cold storage, transport, and retail into a learning optimization loop. Uncertainty in demand, lead times, capacities, spoilage, and emissions is modeled using adaptive fuzzy sets, while a deep-learning surrogate accelerates a multi-objective NSGA-II optimizer to co-design decisions across cost, CO₂e, and resilience. In a perishable dairy case, the hybrid approach reduces total cost by 12.2%, lowers emissions by 15.2%, and raises the resilience index by 22.5% relative to the Fuzzy–AI model without Digital Twin integration. The optimizer stabilizes in ∼35 generations, and under severe disruptions the network recovers to 95% capacity in ∼5 h (vs. >10 h traditionally). Conceptually, the framework operationalizes resilience via adaptability (sensing disruptions, simulating alternatives, and reallocating resources in real time) rather than costly redundancy. Managerially, it enables simulate-before-implement orchestration and transparent cost–carbon–resilience trade-offs aligned with Scope-3 reporting. The results indicate that digital twins combined with fuzzy reasoning and learning assisted optimization can deliver simultaneously lower cost, lower emissions, and higher resilience for perishable food chains.

title: Microsoft Excel As a Tool for Digitizing Financial Records and Supporting Decision-Making Among MSMEs in Dharmasraya Regency in The Era of Digital Transformation
summary: This study aims to understand the use of Microsoft Excel as a tool for digitalizing financial records and supporting decision-making among micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in Dharmasraya Regency. The study focuses on transaction-recording practices, the use of financial information for operational decisions, perceived benefits, challenges, and support needs. It is designed as a descriptive qualitative field study. Primary data are planned to be collected through semi-structured interviews with MSME owners or managers, observation of bookkeeping practices, and authorized documentation. Secondary data include government statistics, local planning documents, accounting standards, and scholarly articles on Excel-based financial reporting for MSMEs. Data analysis will involve data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. Existing literature indicates that spreadsheets can support transaction recording and financial summaries; however, their practical value depends on complete data entry, user understanding, formula checking, and file security. As primary field data have not yet been incorporated into this draft, these statements provide a conceptual basis that must be examined through field research in Dharmasraya

title: Linking digital marketing capabilities, innovation and firm performance in emerging B2B markets: evidence from Togo
summary: Purpose This study aims to investigate the relationships among digital marketing capabilities (DMCs), innovation, firm performance and environmental dynamism in business-to-business (B2B) small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in Togo. Drawing on Dynamic Capabilities Theory, it examines whether innovation mediates the relationship between DMCs and firm performance and whether environmental dynamism moderates the innovation–performance relationship. By focusing on an underexplored African emerging economy characterized by institutional constraints and limited digital maturity, the study seeks to extend understanding of how DMCs create value and improve competitiveness in structurally constrained B2B environments. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was adopted to examine the relationships among DMCs, innovation, firm performance and environmental dynamism in Togolese B2B SMEs. Data were collected from 220 legally registered SMEs operating across Togo. The data were analyzed using exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, and structural equation modelling. Hayes’ PROCESS macro was used to test the proposed mediation and moderation effects. Given the cross-sectional design, potential reverse causality and unobserved firm-level factors cannot be fully excluded, and the findings are therefore interpreted as supporting the hypothesized relationships rather than establishing definitive causal effects. Findings The findings show that DMCs positively influence firm performance and innovation. Innovation also positively influences firm performance and significantly mediates the relationship between DMCs and firm performance. However, environmental dynamism does not significantly moderate the relationship between innovation and firm performance. These findings support the proposed relationships among DMCs, innovation and firm performance and highlight innovation as an important mechanism through which DMCs contribute to performance. Given the cross-sectional design, the findings should be interpreted with caution regarding causal inference. Originality/value This study extends the digital marketing and Dynamic Capabilities literature by providing evidence from an underexplored African B2B context. Rather than offering only a contextual contribution, it demonstrates how DMCs create value through innovation under conditions of institutional fragility and resource constraints. The study also clarifies the mediating role of innovation while showing that environmental dynamism does not significantly alter the innovation–performance relationship. By examining these relationships in Togolese SMEs, the research broadens understanding of digital transformation in emerging markets and identifies important boundary conditions for applying Dynamic Capabilities Theory in structurally constrained environments.

title: Blockchain Enabled Decentralized Nuclear Waste Supply Chain Management
summary: As nuclear waste has long-term effects on the environment and society, managing it safely and effectively is a major global concern. Conventional nuclear waste management systems may face challenges related to record keeping, transparency, and reliance on manual monitoring, potentially affecting operational efficiency and stakeholder confidence. This study presents a blockchain-based platform designed to enhance accountability, data integrity, and traceability in nuclear waste management procedures. The proposed system leverages the decentralized and tamper-resistant nature of blockchain technology to record and track waste-related information throughout its lifecycle. It provides a user-friendly interface to support interaction among stakeholders, including waste producers, storage facilities, and the general public. The system's development and testing demonstrate the implementation of blockchain-based record keeping, waste tracking, and sensor data monitoring. These functionalities provide a foundation for maintaining verifiable records and improving the visibility of waste management activities. Although the current evaluation demonstrates the system's functional capabilities, further comparative testing is required to quantify improvements in data integrity, traceability, and operational efficiency over conventional approaches. This project contributes to ongoing efforts toward safer and more sustainable nuclear waste management by presenting a potential solution that can be further evaluated and adapted for other hazardous material management applications.

title: GREEN SUPPLY CHAIN MANAGEMENT AND FIRM PERFORMANCE IN E-COMMERCE ENTERPRISES
summary: Drawing on the resource - based view and natural resource - based view, this study examines how green supply chain management practices influence the performance of e - Commerce enterprises. This study conceptualizes green supply chain management through five di mensions: intra - organizational environmental management, product eco - design, green supplier integration, green customer cooperation, and reverse logistics. The study further investigates the role of environmental performance in improving operational, econo mic, and social performance. Using a quantitative approach with partial least squares structural equation modeling, the study collected survey data from 162 managers and employees in e - Commerce enterprises. The results indicate that all five dimensions of green supply chain management practices positively affect environmental performance. Environmental performance subsequently enhances operational, economic, and social performance, while operational performance significantly and positively affects economic performance. However, social performance does not directly affect economic performance. The study contributes to theory by extending the resource - based view and natural resource - based view to the underexplored e - Commerce context. The results also suggest t hat e - Commerce enterprises should invest in eco - design, environmental management systems, supplier collaboration, customer engagement, and reverse - logistics capabilities to improve sustainability and competitiveness.

title: Pharmaceutical Shortages as a Multi-Level Governance Failure: An Exploratory Multi- Stakeholder Qualitative Study with Implications for EU and UK Policy
summary: Abstract Background Medicine shortages increasingly threaten patient safety and health system resilience across high-income countries. Despite expanding literature on supply chain vulnerabilities, the perspectives of frontline professionals, such as pharmacists and clinicians, remain underrepresented, and the multi-level governance dimensions of shortage management remain underexplored. Methods We held a participatory multi-stakeholder workshop in March 2025 at the Università di Bologna, Italy. Eighteen participants from the UK and Italy took part in structured presentations and facilitated discussions. They included clinicians, pharmacists, procurement specialists, policymakers, industry representatives, and academic researchers. Recordings of the discussions were transcribed, anonymised, and analysed using thematic analysis in NVivo 15, with themes interpreted through a multi-level governance framework. Results Five themes were identified: diversification and cooperation; transparency and trust; regulatory frameworks; demand-side pressures and public messaging; and national and regional security. Participants highlighted geographic concentration of manufacturing, fragmented supply chain communication, and rigid regulatory frameworks as structural causes of medicines shortages. Frontline professionals, particularly community pharmacists, were identified as bearing the greatest operational burden of shortages while having the least regulatory flexibility to respond. Proposed responses included expanded domestic manufacturing, real-time inventory systems, reformed procurement criteria, greater pharmacist dispensing flexibility, and strengthened international coordination. Conclusions Our findings indicate that pharmaceutical shortages represent a systemic, multi-level governance failure rather than a purely logistical problem. Effective responses require coordinated action across supranational, national, and local levels. This should include regulatory reform such as expanded pharmacist dispensing flexibility; improved transparency and incentive-based early notification; and strategic investment in supply chain resilience to facilitate cross-sector stock redistribution. Reshoring and diversification strategies must also engage with the environmental governance implications of where and how medicines are manufactured. Our findings provide preliminary practitioner-informed evidence relevant to EU and UK policy developments to address medicine shortages, including the Critical Medicines Act (CMA), while highlighting persistent gaps in their scope.

title: Le nouveau modèle de développement et la gouvernance territoriale : Enjeux de la régionalisation avancée et rôle de la communication publique au Maroc
summary: Résumé Cet article analyse la contribution du Nouveau Modèle de Développement (NMD) à la transformation de la gouvernance territoriale au Maroc dans le contexte de la régionalisation avancée, en accordant une attention particulière au rôle de la communication publique. L’étude adopte une approche qualitative fondée sur une analyse documentaire de rapports institutionnels, de textes réglementaires et de travaux scientifiques portant sur le NMD, la décentralisation, la gouvernance territoriale et la participation citoyenne. Les résultats montrent que le NMD contribue à renforcer la territorialisation des politiques publiques, la déconcentration administrative, les capacités des acteurs territoriaux et la transformation numérique. La communication publique apparaît comme un levier transversal permettant d’améliorer la transparence, la participation citoyenne et la coordination entre les différents niveaux de gouvernance. Une analyse SWOT de la région Drâa-Tafilalet met en évidence d’importantes potentialités territoriales, notamment dans les énergies renouvelables et l’économie locale, mais également des contraintes liées aux infrastructures, à la fracture numérique et à la coordination institutionnelle. L’étude souligne ainsi que la réussite de la régionalisation avancée dépend d’une gouvernance multiniveaux efficace, d’une communication publique adaptée aux réalités territoriales, d’une digitalisation inclusive et du renforcement du capital humain.Mots clés : Nouveau Modèle de Développement ; gouvernance territoriale ; régionalisation avancée ; communication publique ; participation citoyenne ; Maroc. Abstract This article examines the contribution of Morocco’s New Development Model (NDM) to the transformation of territorial governance within the framework of advanced regionalization, with particular attention to the role of public communication. The study adopts a qualitative approach based on a documentary analysis of institutional reports, regulatory documents, and scientific literature addressing the NDM, decentralization, territorial governance, and citizen participation. The findings indicate that the NDM contributes to strengthening the territorialization of public policies, administrative deconcentration, local actors’ capacities, and digital transformation. Public communication emerges as a cross-cutting governance mechanism that can enhance transparency, citizen participation, and coordination across different levels of government. A SWOT analysis of the Drâa-Tafilalet region highlights significant territorial assets, particularly in renewable energy and the local economy, while revealing persistent challenges related to infrastructure, the digital divide, and institutional coordination. The study concludes that the success of advanced regionalization depends on effective multilevel governance, territorially adapted public communication, inclusive digitalization, and stronger human capital at the local and regional levels.Keywords New Development Model; territorial governance; advanced regionalization; public communication; citizen participation; Morocco.

title: Mécanismes de gouvernance et performance financière des sociétés anonymes à actionnaire unique étatique en République Démocratique du Congo : étude critique du cas de GECAMINES SA
summary: Résumé Cette recherche examine l’influence des mécanismes de gouvernance prévus par le droit congolais sur la performance financière de GECAMINES SA, entreprise publique stratégique du secteur minier en République Démocratique du Congo. Dans un contexte de paradoxe entre richesse minérale et pauvreté persistante, elle s’appuie sur un cadre théorique combinant la théorie de l’agence, la théorie institutionnelle et celle des parties prenantes. Six hypothèses ont été formulées autour de l’application partielle des normes, de l’efficacité des organes de contrôle, de l’ingérence politique, de la faiblesse de la reddition des comptes, de la perception managériale de la performance et des contraintes institutionnelles. L’approche qualitative, de type étude de cas interprétative, repose sur douze entretiens semi-directifs et mobilise des outils d’analyse lexicométrique (CHD, AFC, ADS) via IRaMuTeQ. Elle met en évidence un décalage profond entre les prescriptions légales et les pratiques effectives, traduisant une gouvernance affaiblie. Les résultats confirment les hypothèses, en soulignant la fragilité des structures de contrôle, la faible autonomie décisionnelle et la persistance des interférences politiques dans la gestion de l’entreprise. L’étude propose des recommandations pour renforcer l’autonomie des organes de direction, améliorer la transparence financière et moderniser les outils de gestion. L’étude insiste sur la nécessité d’une refondation de la gouvernance publique, orientée vers la création de valeur, la légitimité institutionnelle et la souveraineté économique. Mots clés : gouvernance d’entreprise ; entreprise publique ; performance financière ; Gécamines SA ; droit congolais. Abstract This study examines how the governance mechanisms provided for under Congolese law affect the financial performance of GECAMINES SA, a strategic state-owned mining company in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Against the backdrop of the “paradox of plenty”, in which vast mineral wealth coexists with persistent poverty, the study draws on a theoretical framework combining agency theory, institutional theory and stakeholder theory. Six hypotheses were formulated, relating to the partial implementation of legal norms, the effectiveness of oversight bodies, political interference, weak accountability, managers’ perceptions of performance and institutional constraints. A qualitative, interpretive single-case design was adopted, based on twelve semi-structured interviews analysed with the IRaMuTeQ software through Reinert’s descending hierarchical classification, correspondence analysis and similarity analysis. The findings reveal a substantial gap between legal requirements and actual practice, indicative of weakened governance. All six hypotheses are supported: control structures remain fragile, decision-making autonomy is limited and political interference in the company’s management persists. The study recommends strengthening the autonomy of governing bodies, enhancing financial transparency and modernising management tools. It concludes that public-sector governance needs to be fundamentally rebuilt around value creation, institutional legitimacy and economic sovereignty. Keywords: corporate governance; state-owned enterprise; financial performance; Gécamines SA; Congolese law.

title: Do Big4 accounting firms affect foreign individuals’ investment decisions? Evidence from an emerging market
summary: Purpose This paper focuses on an emerging market and investigates whether a firm’s audit engagement with a Big4 accounting firm is associated with foreign individuals’ investments. We hypothesize that Big4 accounting firms’ reputation may function as a heuristic trust signal for these investors. Design/methodology/approach We tested our hypothesis by utilizing 225 non-financial firms listed on Borsa Istanbul. The dataset covers 2005 to 2023 and contains 3,590 firm-year observations. Findings Our empirical evidence indicates that foreign individuals are more likely to invest in BIST-listed firms audited by a Big4 accounting firm (AF). Our results are consistent with prior studies showing that accounting firms’ reputation is associated with investors’ decisions. Our robustness analysis suggests that Big4 AFs’ reputation may lose importance when public governance declines. Research limitations/implications The primary limitation of this research is that investor-level data are not publicly available. We also did not incorporate audit-firm-level variables such as expertise and number of partners. Practical implications Our study has implications for managers, policymakers and accounting professionals. Managers seeking to signal trust to foreign individuals may consider the positive association between Big4 AF engagement and foreign investment. Social implications Policymakers should consider measures to enhance public governance quality to attract more foreign individuals to Borsa Istanbul. Big4 AFs should note that this reputational advantage weakens as public governance declines. Originality/value While prior studies have examined institutional investors’ and mutual funds’ preferences for Big4 accounting firms, this study contributes new archival evidence on foreign individual investors’ equity investment decisions in relation to Big4 engagement in an emerging market context.

title: Using Financial Accounting Information to Estimate the Income Shifting of US Multinationals
summary: ABSTRACT Existing estimates of how much income US multinational corporations (MNCs) shift out of the United States differ dramatically, and most cannot identify which specific firms do the shifting. We use data from firms' public financial reports to derive firm‐year estimates of US MNCs' outbound income shifting. We find that aggregate US outbound income shifting is substantially lower than widely cited macroeconomic‐based estimates, with the gap driven primarily by double counting of foreign income in macroeconomic data rather than by differences in firms' sensitivity to tax rates. Income shifting is also highly concentrated among a small number of firms, primarily in intangible‐intensive industries such as computers and pharmaceuticals, while most MNCs shift little or no income. This concentration implies that size‐based thresholds embedded in the OECD's Pillar 2 and the US corporate alternative minimum tax will capture the most active income shifters but may also impose compliance burdens on many firms that shift minimal income. These findings have direct implications for policy‐makers designing international tax rules, tax authorities prioritizing audit resources toward high‐risk income shifters, and investors and lenders assessing MNCs' tax‐related exposures.

title: The Influence of Board Characteristics, ESG-Linked Compensation, and ESG Controversy on ESG Performance: Does the Presence of the ESG Committee Matter?
summary: This study aims to empirically examine the influence of board gender diversity, board independence, ESG-linked compensation, and ESG controversies on ESG performance. Additionally, it seeks to empirically investigate the moderating role of an ESG committee. The study focuses on all non-financial companies listed on the stock exchanges of the ASEAN-5 countries, which consists of Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand for which data are available via the LSEG (Refinitiv) Eikon database, covering 700 data of the period from 2019 to 2025. Employing multiple regression analysis and also moderated regression analysis, the study provides empirical evidence of the positive influence of board independence, ESG-linked compensation, and ESG controversies on ESG performance. Regarding the moderating role of an ESG committee, the findings indicate that such a committee strengthens the positive impact of board gender diversity on ESG performance. Furthermore, the committee is shown to mitigate the negative impact of ESG controversies on ESG performance.

title: Hospitality Raw Material Distribution Logistics and Supply Contract Certainty Reconstruction in Frontier 3T Regions: Empirical Case of Krui, Pesisir Barat
summary: Background: Tourism accommodation operators in Krui suffer from fragile overland fresh supply chains, erratic delivery schedules, and verbal agreements lacking enforceability. Objectives: To reconstruct contractual certainty under Articles 1320 and 1338 of the Indonesian Civil Code while optimizing multi-stop fresh produce distribution. Methods: Comprehensive field study across 40 hospitality operators in Tanjung Setia, Mandiri Beach, and Krui City with route optimization modeling. Results: Formalizing Service Level Agreements with stipulated liquidated damages (Article 1243) reduces supply disruption frequency by 54% and cuts aggregate logistical overhead by 22.8%. Conclusion: Demonstrates that legal enforceability is an indispensable prerequisite for supply chain resilience in emerging remote tourism clusters. title: Does Eco‐Efficiency Pay in a Fragmented Food Industry? A Simultaneous‐Equations Analysis of Accounting‐Based Resource Productivity and Profitability in the Italian Dairy Sector
summary: ABSTRACT This study asks whether eco‐efficiency and environmental investment relate to firm financial performance in the Italian dairy industry, and whether that relationship is reciprocal rather than one‐directional, across the 2020–2024 energy‐ and input‐price cycle. Using audited AIDA accounts for the population of 466 limited companies in ATECO division 10.5 (463 firms with usable accounts, 2278 firm‐years; 324 industrial processors and 138 artisanal dairies), it measures eco‐efficiency through an accounting‐based resource‐productivity proxy (revenue per unit of tangible capital), complements it with process‐modernisation capital and recorded green‐innovation intensities and with external life‐cycle benchmarks, and estimates a two‐equation simultaneous system by three‐stage least squares with equation‐specific instruments that pass over‐identification tests, firm‐clustered standard errors and controls for cooperative governance, PDO area and product segment. The sector is extremely fragmented (Herfindahl–Hirschman index 0.013), and one third of its firms are producer cooperatives. The estimates are consistent with a reciprocal relationship: Resource productivity is robustly associated with higher return on assets across pooled, fixed‐effects and first‐difference instrumental‐variable estimators, whereas the feedback from profitability to resource productivity holds in levels and within firms but not in first‐difference instrumental‐variable estimates, so the reciprocal reading is supported but not established. Process‐modernisation capital shows no contemporaneous association with margins, recorded green innovation is negligible (zero in 90.6% of firm‐years), and cooperatives are as resource‐productive as investor‐owned firms but retain none of the gain as margin, in line with the member‐price‐maximisation logic of cooperative governance. Unlike neighbouring shock‐hit food chains, dairy delivered growth with margins. The paper contributes a full‐population, audited‐accounts test of the eco‐efficiency–performance relationship in a cooperative‐dense, fragmented food industry, documents a measurement inversion in balance‐sheet innovation proxies, and derives implications for environmental strategy, green‐capital allocation and the territorial dairy system.

title: Key audit matters and audit report lag in the Saudi governance context: Does auditor type matter?
summary: This study examines the relationship between key audit matters (KAM) disclosures and audit report lag (ARL) in the Saudi capital market and investigates whether this relationship is moderated by auditor type. Using feasible generalized least squares (FGLS) on a panel dataset of 832 firm-year observations for firms listed on the Saudi Stock Exchange (Tadawul) over the period 2016–2021, the study finds that the number of KAM is positively associated with ARL, consistent with recent studies (Bajary et al., 2025; Cameran & Campa, 2025), suggesting that a greater number of KAM reflects increased audit complexity and audit effort, thereby requiring additional time to complete the audit. The results also show that this relationship is significantly stronger for firms audited by Big 4 auditors (Deloitte, PricewaterhouseCoopers [PwC], Ernst & Young [EY], or KPMG), and insignificant for those audited by non-Big 4 auditors. The findings remain robust across alternative model specifications and variable measurements. The study extends the audit reporting literature by demonstrating that the effect of KAM disclosures on audit report timeliness depends on auditor type. The findings also provide practical implications for regulators, investors, and auditors by highlighting that greater audit transparency through KAM may require additional reporting time and audit effort, particularly for Big 4 auditors.

title: Integrated diagnostics of adaptive digital transformation in FMCG retail
summary: The article develops an integrated diagnostic model of adaptive digital transformation in FMCG retail aimed at identifying imbalances between technological development, organizational capabilities, and market outcomes. The proposed approach combines four interrelated diagnostic contours: external digital opportunities, actual technology adoption, internal digital readiness, and customer and market response. The research is based on system, process, comparative, and structural-logical approaches, as well as analysis, synthesis, classification, and scientific generalization. The empirical illustration of the model uses publicly available corporate data for 2025-2026 covering ten Russian FMCG retail chains. Digital readiness is assessed through four components: management commitment, digital potential, digital culture, and digital strategy. The results indicate that relatively balanced average levels of digital readiness coexist with noticeable firm-level differences in their internal configuration. Digital culture demonstrates the highest average value (0.885), whereas digital strategy has the lowest (0.840), suggesting that the development of technological and organizational capabilities may outpace their integration into a coherent long-term transformation agenda. To translate diagnostic results into managerial decisions, a matrix linking specific diagnostic signals with corresponding management responses is proposed. The developed framework supports the identification of capability bottlenecks, underused technologies, customer-journey friction, and inconsistencies between digital readiness and actual technology adoption. Its practical application can facilitate the prioritization of digital initiatives, continuous monitoring, strategic adjustment, control, and recurrent recalibration of digital transformation trajectories in FMCG retail enterprises.

title: A Multilevel Socio-Technical System: Formation of Government Financial Reporting Quality in China—Survey Evidence from the 2019 Accrual Accounting Reform
summary: Using questionnaire data collected in 2019, this study examines how preparation conditions relate to perceived government financial reporting quality (GFRQ) in the first year of China’s new government accounting system. The multilevel socio-technical systems (MSTS) framework distinguishes departmental reporting as an operational layer and consolidated reporting as an integration layer. Separate respondent-level regressions use 5157 departmental and 672 consolidated questionnaires; they estimate associations within each report type, without testing interactions or information transmission between layers. Policy cognition and institutional support, and information systems and data integration are positively associated with GFRQ in both samples. Accounting foundation and accrual implementation are significant in the departmental sample. The prespecified coordination and supervision index is positive in both baseline models, although departmental inference is sensitive to scoring. These findings describe preparation conditions and quality evaluations in the 2019 survey. Comparisons across report types are descriptive; coefficient equality has not been formally tested. Cross-layer transmission and feedback remain theoretical propositions, while suggestions on responsibility tracing, reconciliation and error correction are directions for subsequent evaluation. The results are bounded by the survey’s institutional and technical context and do not establish later reform outcomes or current governance performance.

title: The Effect of Local Own-Source Revenue and Capital Expenditure on Local Government Financial Performance: The Moderating Role of Financial Reporting Quality
summary: Indonesian local governments have expanded own-source revenue and capital budgets and mostly earn favorable audit opinions, yet their expenditure-to-revenue ratios remain near or above 100 percent. Prior studies report conflicting effects of revenue and capital spending and rarely test whether financial reporting quality conditions them. This study examines how own-source revenue and capital expenditure affect local government financial performance and whether reporting quality moderates these effects, drawing on fiscal decentralization, agency, and stewardship theories. We analyzed a balanced panel of 15 regencies and municipalities in Lampung Province from 2018 to 2024 (105 observations) using pooled regression with moderated regression analysis. Own-source revenue significantly raises the expenditure-to-revenue ratio (coefficient 15.07, p = 0.006), showing that revenue growth without discipline expands spending rather than efficiency. Capital expenditure and audit-based reporting quality have no significant direct effects at the 5 percent level. Reporting quality is a pure moderator: its negative interaction with revenue (coefficient −4.06, p = 0.007) reverses the marginal effect of revenue from +2.90 under qualified opinions to −1.15 under unqualified opinions. Audit compliance therefore disciplines spending only when revenue expands. It does not moderate capital expenditure, and the model explains only 8.2 percent of variance, so the results are conditional rather than general. The study contributes by modeling reporting quality as an institutional boundary condition in fiscal decentralization and by separating compliance from efficiency. Policymakers should pair revenue mobilization with expenditure controls and use audited statements for budget monitoring rather than as compliance targets.

title: From orchestrated resources to supply chain performance: the indirect role of power
summary: Purpose The study applied resource orchestration and resource dependency theories to examine how firm resources affect supply chain performance in Ghana's food and beverage industry, as well as the mediating role of power. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative research approach and explanatory design were employed using survey data collected from firms in Ghana's food and beverage sector. Out of the 427 questionnaires distributed, 395 usable responses were obtained. The data were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling to assess direct and specific indirect effects. Findings The results indicate that human, financial and innovation resources significantly enhance supply chain performance, whereas relational and structural resources do not exert direct effects. Power positively influences performance and serves as a critical mechanism, with both partial and full mediation observed across resource categories. The findings reveal that resource value is heterogeneous and context-dependent, and that performance gains are realised when resources are effectively translated into influence that aligns with partner behaviour. Originality/value The study advances the literature by moving beyond the composite view of firm resources and demonstrating that resource effects are not uniform but context-specific. It further positions power as a central mechanism linking resource deployment to performance, offering a more context-sensitive explanation of supply chain dynamics in developing economies.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Food Supply Chains: Distribution Optimization and Waste Reduction
summary: One-third of the food made for people to eat gets. Thrown away but the tools used to fight this issue mostly only look at how well we can predict it (Onyeaka et al. 2025). This chapter says that just predicting won't cut down on loss. Waste happens at points where decisions are made. How much to restock when to send out goods how to divide up products when to lower prices and how to get rid of things. These points aren’t fixed just by better predictions. The chapter connects three ways of looking at the problem with the real-life ways that fresh food ends up being thrown guessing how much people will want figuring out how long food will last based on basic chemistry and temperature effects and planning how to deliver food in a way that deals with it being perishable time limits and pollution. The proof includes a 14.8% drop in food waste per store and 26,705 tonnes of CO₂ not released because of AI in stores (Onyeaka et al. 2025) predicting how long food will last with changing storage conditions (Rashvand et al., 2025) using AI to watch and support recycling efforts (Onyeaka et al. 2023) and a look at 104 studies about food loss before it gets to people between 2015 and 2024 (Ma et al. 2026) that showed prevention isn’t getting much attention as fixing things later. Three main points are made: that knowing what is happening matching loss with solutions keeping limits and making sure everyone has the right reasons to help together set limits on what AI can do; that expanding the cold chain is only worth it if the extra energy needed is less than the waste it stops; and that when people say something is good, for the environment they need to say exactly what they mean show how sure they are and tell where the waste is really going.

title: Digital Traceability and Halal Supply Chain Assurance: Building Consumer Trust in Islamic Tourism and Hospitality
summary: Halal tourism and hospitality depend on more than the availability of Muslim-friendly facilities: consumers must be able to trust that food, ingredients, handling practices, accommodation services, and related experiences conform to the standards they expect. Digital traceability technologies—including blockchain-enabled records, QR-linked product information, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, digital certification registries, and interoperable data platforms—can make supply-chain evidence more accessible and strengthen assurance across fragmented service networks. Yet technology does not automatically produce trustworthy halal outcomes. Inaccurate source data, weak governance, inconsistent certification, privacy concerns, and poor consumer-facing communication can undermine the credibility of digital systems. The analysis proposes that traceability affects trust primarily through perceived transparency and assurance credibility, with certification governance and platform interoperability shaping the strength of these relationships. The article also identifies risks associated with “technology-washing,” fragmented standards, and the mistaken assumption that immutable records guarantee truthful inputs. It concludes with a set of testable hypotheses, an empirical research design, and strategic implications for destination managers, hospitality firms, halal certifiers, technology providers, and Islamic finance stakeholders.

title: Decomposing the Short and Long‐Run Effects of ESG Performance and Materiality on Corporate External Financing Needs
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines the impact of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) performance on corporate external financing needs (EFN), using a global panel comprising 3437 firms and 11,075 firm‐year observations. Drawing on theories from institutional, risk management and behavioral finance, we decompose short‐ and long‐run dynamics using correlated random effects models, addressing endogeneity through two‐stage least squares (2SLS) estimations. Our findings show that higher ESG performance significantly reduces EFN, with the greatest benefits accruing over the long term. Formal mediation analysis reveals that this relationship operates through four economic channels: enhanced asset tangibility, improved free cash flow generation, eased financial constraints and superior investment efficiency. A key contribution of this study is the identification of a U‐shaped relationship between the materiality of ESG reporting and EFN. Above an optimal threshold, information overload and compliance costs dominate, thereby increasing EFN. We also document that the mitigating effect of ESG varies across pillars and time horizons. These results emphasize the temporal, contingent and mechanism‐driven nature of ESG in corporate financing, providing actionable guidance for managers and policymakers seeking to align sustainability practices with financial resilience.

title: Future‐ready blood services: Building strategic foresight for the blood supply chain
summary: BACKGROUND: Blood is an irreplaceable resource in the healthcare system, and ensuring its safe and timely delivery from donors to patients is the core function of the blood supply chain (BSC). Managing the BSC is increasingly challenging given the uncertainty surrounding interconnected factors such as demographic shifts, technological advances, and evolving clinical practices. Conventional planning approaches are insufficient to capture these complexities, motivating the development of narrative scenarios. STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: We developed narrative scenarios for the BSC using a decomposition-based scenario development framework. Through a systematic literature review and expert consultations, we identified 10 key uncertainty factors and defined four development paths for each. We elicited pairwise consistency ratings between development paths from BSC experts and used them to select four internally consistent and maximally diverse scenarios. RESULTS: Four internally consistent scenarios were developed: Strained Resilience, Thriving Transformation, Adaptive Automation, and Regulatory Rigidity. Cross-scenario analysis reveals three structural findings: (i) where synthetic blood alternatives emerge, they complement rather than replace voluntary donation, (ii) apparent stability can mask underlying fragility, and (iii) long-term resilience is determined by social and institutional conditions rather than operational capacity alone. CONCLUSION: Our findings identify donor engagement, institutional trust, cybersecurity resilience, and regulatory agility as robust strategic priorities for the BSC across a wide range of possible futures. The scenarios reveal that factors conventionally excluded from BSC analytical models, such as civic trust and regulatory flexibility, are among the most consequential drivers of long-term system resilience.

title: Adaptive and Distributed Leadership for Digital Transformation: Building Resilient and Connected School Systems
summary: Digital transformation challenges school leaders to maintain continuity, respond to technological change, and coordinate collective action. Objective: This study explored how adaptive and distributed leadership were practiced by school leaders, how these practices were perceived to strengthen resilient and connected school systems, and the challenges and opportunities encountered. Methods: A qualitative descriptive design was used with eight school leaders from the Caloocan North II District, Schools Division of Caloocan City, during school year 2025–2026. Data were generated through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using the thematic approach identified in the source dissertation as Boyatzis’ approach. Results: The analysis organized participants’ accounts into three overarching themes: (1) adaptive and distributed leadership as foundations for collaborative digital transformation; (2) shared leadership practices as foundations of school resilience and connectedness; and (3) challenges and opportunities in applying these leadership approaches during digital transformation. Described practices included responsiveness to teacher readiness, revising digital plans, piloting tools, delegation, communication, and peer coaching. Reported constraints included resistance to change, unreliable connectivity, limited devices, and uneven digital competence. Conclusion: Participants described adaptability and shared responsibility as useful strategies for coordinating digital initiatives and sustaining school operations amid disruption. A seven-area leadership development program was proposed; its effectiveness was not evaluated in this study.

title: Product liability of e-commerce marketplaces in India: law, judicial trends, and policy alternatives
summary: This paper examines the product liability of e-commerce marketplaces in India under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. While the Act introduced a statutory framework for product liability, its application to online platforms like Amazon and Flipkart remains legally ambiguous. The paper argues against imposing liability on these marketplaces, as they lack substantial control over product design, quality, or safety-factors central to the evolution of product liability law. It analyses key business models, statutory provisions, and decisions by Indian consumer forums, revealing a pro-consumer bias unsupported by legal reasoning. Comparative insights from the United States and European Union further demonstrate that general platform liability is not the global norm. As an alternative, the paper proposes asymmetric mandatory insurance for third-party sellers exceeding a specified sales threshold. This solution is general in nature, applicable to all jurisdictions. This mechanism offers a pragmatic way to compensate consumers without stifling innovation. On a broader level, this paper contributes to the evolving legal discourse on consumer protection in the digital economy.

title: Cross-Border Ownership and Input Access: Evidence from the Lithium Supply Chain
summary: How does cross-border ownership shape the lithium supply chain? Using global data on mines and refineries, I estimate a model in which ownership can lower refiners' effective ore costs, encourage mines to restrict spot sales, and soften competition. To study these effects, I examine policies motivated by national security concerns about reliable access to critical mineral inputs: divestiture of Chinese stakes in overseas producers and a ban on ore exports to China. Divestiture increases spot ore supply but leaves lithium output nearly unchanged, while continued trade preserves Chinese access to ore. The export ban reduces global lithium supply because refining capacity elsewhere cannot fully replace lost Chinese production. Ownership transfers do not reserve ore for domestic production; restricting Chinese access imposes a substantial supply cost at existing capacities.

title: Forensic Accounting in the Digital Asset Era: A Structured Framework for Bitcoin Verification and Investigation
summary: The rise of blockchain-based digital assets presents significant challenges for auditors tasked with ensuring compliance with the International Standards on Auditing. Traditional audit methods are often ill-equipped to address the decentralised, pseudonymous and cryptographically complex nature of the asset class. This study develops an Assertion-based Audit Framework as a structured audit artefact tailored to the technical attributes of the Bitcoin blockchain. Using a methodology embedded in the design sciences paradigm, this research applied an elaborated Action Design Research approach to iteratively design and validate the audit framework in collaboration with industry professionals. It translates blockchain protocol features, such as unspent transaction outputs, public and private key cryptography, and decentralised ledger systems into assertion-level audit procedures covering existence, rights and obligations, completeness, valuation, accuracy, occurrence and cut-off. As illustrated in the simulated context, the envisaged audit framework aims to provide reliable and reproducible evidence, thereby strengthening the audit quality and forensic investigations involving bitcoin. This research advances both academic and professional knowledge by offering a formalised, technology-integrated audit framework, with broader implications for auditing digital assets across various blockchain protocols – supporting both regulatory-compliant financial audits and forensic investigations conducted where robust and verifiable evidence is essential.

title: Akses Green Finance bagi UMKM di Indonesia: Hambatan Struktural, Kesesuaian Instrumen, dan Strategi Penguatan melalui Narrative Literature Review
summary: Aims: This study aims to analyze access to green finance among micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) in Indonesia by identifying structural barriers, enabling factors, and the suitability of green financing instruments for MSMEs’ characteristics and stages of green practice adoption. It also develops a conceptual framework to explain the interaction between MSMEs’ internal readiness, financial institutions’ assessment mechanisms, and policy ecosystem support in expanding access to green finance. Method: This study employs a narrative literature review approach. Relevant literature was retrieved through Google Scholar and GARUDA, while publication metadata were cross-checked through Crossref. A critical thematic analysis was conducted on relevant scholarly articles, regulations, and institutional reports to identify recurring barriers, evaluate the suitability of financing instruments, and synthesize strategies for strengthening MSMEs’ access to green finance in Indonesia. Results: The findings indicate that barriers to green finance access emerge from the interaction of three dimensions. First, the internal MSME dimension includes limited financial and environmental literacy, inadequate financial record-keeping, administrative constraints, and limited capacity to bear the upfront costs of green investment. Second, the financial institution dimension involves collateral requirements, risk assessment practices, transaction costs, and the limited availability of financing instruments suited to MSMEs’ scale of operations. Third, the policy ecosystem dimension encompasses the clarity of green business criteria, credit guarantee support, business assistance, and digital infrastructure. The review also finds that evidence concerning digital literacy and fintech utilization primarily explains the adoption of green practices rather than direct access to financing. Therefore, financing access, green practice adoption, and business performance should be treated as distinct outcomes. Novelty: The novelty of this study lies in developing a three-layer conceptual framework that integrates MSMEs’ readiness, financial institutions’ assessment mechanisms, and policy ecosystem support, while distinguishing financing access from green practice adoption and business performance. The framework emphasizes the importance of aligning financing instruments with MSMEs’ characteristics and stages of green adoption. In practical terms, proportionate financing requirements, credit guarantees, financial and environmental assistance, and evaluation indicators covering applications, approvals, rejections, access costs, and environmental benefits should be developed. The proposed framework remains conceptual and therefore requires empirical testing using actual financing data.

title: Digital transformation and marketing synergy in the sustainable development of tourism enterprise
summary: In the modern era, the rapid and continuous development of digital technologies has had a significant and multidimensional impact on the management systems, marketing strategies, and customer relationship management of enterprises operating in the tourism sector. The concept of digital transformation is not limited to the implementation of new technological solutions; it also requires the reconfiguration of organizational culture, employee behavior patterns, internal and external communication mechanisms, and social interactions in accordance with the modern digital environment. This process necessitates the adoption of more flexible management approaches in tourism enterprises and creates conditions for improving both internal efficiency and customer-oriented service quality. The main purpose of this study is to comprehensively examine the interrelationships between organizational behavior, social interaction, and marketing synergy in tourism enterprises, as well as to determine the impact of these factors on overall marketing performance. The article analyzes, from theoretical and conceptual perspectives, the influence of organizational behavior patterns and social interactions on marketing outcomes in the context of digital transformation. The research findings indicate that enhancing employee motivation, improving leadership quality, establishing effective internal and external communication systems, and integrating digital marketing tools within a unified strategy play a crucial role in strengthening the competitiveness and market position of tourism enterprises. Furthermore, the interaction of these factors enables organizations to increase customer satisfaction, ensure service personalization, and create longterm loyalty.

title: Risk Return Dynamics and Portfolio Performance of Islamic Microfinance Institutions: Evidence from Post-Digital Transformation Era
summary: Digital transformation is reshaping the operating models of Islamic microfinance institutions (IMFIs), changing how they originate financing, monitor clients, process payments, and manage portfolio risk. Yet the financial consequences of digital adoption remain ambiguous. Digital channels can reduce transaction costs, expand outreach, and improve the timeliness of credit information, but they can also introduce cyber risk, model risk, operational concentration, and new forms of borrower over-indebtedness. This article develops a risk-return framework for evaluating IMFIs after digital transformation, with particular attention to the interaction between Shariah-compliant financing, portfolio quality, operating efficiency, and digital capability. Drawing on financial intermediation theory, portfolio theory, information asymmetry, institutional theory, and the objectives of Islamic finance, the article proposes a comparative empirical design using institution-level panel data. The framework distinguishes profitability, portfolio quality, liquidity, capital adequacy, outreach, and social performance rather than reducing institutional success to a single accounting ratio. It also treats digital transformation as a capability whose value depends on governance, data quality, staff competence, cybersecurity, and the design of financing contracts. Twelve hypotheses specify expected relationships among digital maturity, risk management, portfolio diversification, non-performing financing, cost efficiency, and risk-adjusted performance. The article’s analytical synthesis suggests that digital adoption is most likely to improve risk-adjusted returns when it is embedded in disciplined underwriting, responsible financing, Shariah governance, and portfolio monitoring. Because no institution-level dataset was supplied, the manuscript presents a theory-driven framework and research protocol rather than fabricated statistical findings.
